taxonomic_note: Accepted by ITIS and World Flora Online; Kew's Ruellia genus backbone lists Ruellia drummondiana as an accepted species. Texas endemic.
look_here_first: Look at the leaf axil. Drummond's ruellia has purple flowers/cymes essentially sessile in the axils rather than raised on a terminal stalk. The ovate leaves and stems have short fine pubescence, not the conspicuous long hairs of R. humilis. If fruit is present, the capsule's only 2–4 seeds are a powerful confirmation.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Travis County — UT Plant Resources Center's Travis County Acanthaceae specimen index includes Ruellia drummondiana; Travis County park inventory also documents a locally abundant wild population. Williamson County — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed field-based county treatment of Ruellia drummondiana. Real County — a verified county-flora study lists Ruellia drummondiana as a newly vouchered Real County record after cross-checking major Texas herbaria.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Texas endemic status does not by itself satisfy the project rule; PASS uses three explicit project counties.

best_field_traits: Texas-endemic perennial herb, decumbent to ascending
opposite ovate to broadly elliptic leaves with acute to obtuse tips
foliage short-pilose/finely pubescent rather than glabrous or long-shaggy
paired axillary cymes essentially sessile, without a long peduncle
violet corolla commonly about 23–32 mm in Williamson material
calyx lobes long, narrow and glandular-hairy
fruit character unusually distinctive: only 2–4 seeds
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Ruellia ciliatiflora: R. ciliatiflora (= R. nudiflora) raises its flowers on conspicuous terminal/upper-axillary peduncles and is much less hairy. Ruellia humilis: Both have nearly sessile axillary flowers, but R. humilis is conspicuously long-pilose with obvious individual hairs along stems and leaf margins; R. drummondiana is finely short-pubescent and has only 2–4 seeds. Ruellia simplex: Mexican petunia has long narrow lanceolate leaves and typically taller, more linear architecture; it is a common non-native landscape escape.
